# Counit of Spectrum Adjunction is a Natural Transformation

## 0. Conventions and definitions

**Frames.** A *frame* is a complete lattice $L$ (bottom $\bot_L$, top $\top_L$, binary meet $\wedge$,
arbitrary join $\bigvee$) which satisfies the *frame distributive law*
$$a \wedge \bigvee S \;=\; \bigvee_{s \in S} (a \wedge s) \qquad (a \in L,\ S \subseteq L).$$
This law is an extra hypothesis: completeness alone does not imply it. (The five-element diamond
$M_3=\{\bot,a,b,c,\top\}$ with $a,b,c$ pairwise incomparable is a complete lattice with
$a\wedge(b\vee c)=a\wedge\top=a \ne \bot=(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge c)$, so it is not a frame.) Accordingly,
every time we assert below that some complete lattice is a frame, we verify the distributive law.

A *frame homomorphism* $h : L \to M$ is a map that preserves finite meets and arbitrary joins:
$$h\Bigl(\bigvee_{s\in S} s\Bigr) = \bigvee_{s\in S} h(s)\quad (S\subseteq L),
\qquad h(a\wedge b) = h(a)\wedge h(b),\qquad h(\top_L)=\top_M .$$
Note the *join* is carried to a *join*, not to a meet. The join clause is asserted for **every** subset
$S\subseteq L$, the empty subset included; since $\bigvee\varnothing=\bot_L$ and $\bigvee\varnothing=\bot_M$,
that instance says exactly $h(\bot_L)=\bot_M$, and it does not follow from the clause for nonempty $S$.
Likewise the empty instance of the meet clause is the separately listed condition $h(\top_L)=\top_M$.
Both empty instances are used below (Lemma 1(c)), so we keep them explicit. A frame homomorphism is monotone,
since $a\le b$ iff $a\vee b=b$. Frames and frame homomorphisms form a category $\mathbf{Frm}$; identities
are identity maps and composition is composition of maps (a composite of frame homomorphisms is again one,
since each clause is preserved by composing).

**Locales.** $\mathbf{Loc} := \mathbf{Frm}^{\mathrm{op}}$. The objects of $\mathbf{Loc}$ are frames; a
$\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f : L \to M$ *is*, by definition, a frame homomorphism in the opposite direction,
which we write $f^{*} : M \to L$. Thus:

* $f \mapsto f^{*}$ is a bijection $\mathbf{Loc}(L,M) \to \mathbf{Frm}(M,L)$; in particular
  $f = g$ in $\mathbf{Loc}$ if and only if $f^{*} = g^{*}$ in $\mathbf{Frm}$;
* $(\mathrm{id}_L)^{*} = \mathrm{id}_L$ and $(g\circ f)^{*} = f^{*}\circ g^{*}$.

We stress that this says only that $\mathbf{Loc}$-*morphisms* are exactly the opposites of frame
homomorphisms. It does **not** say that every such morphism is invertible: $f$ is an isomorphism in
$\mathbf{Loc}$ precisely when $f^{*}$ is an isomorphism (i.e. a bijective) frame homomorphism, which is a
strictly stronger condition. Nothing below requires any $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism to be invertible (see
Remark 6).

**The functor $\mathbf\Omega$.** For a topological space $X=(S,\tau)$ put $\mathbf\Omega X := \tau$,
ordered by $\subseteq$.

*This is a frame.* Arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open, so $\tau$ is a complete
lattice in which $\bigvee \mathcal S = \bigcup\mathcal S$, $U\wedge V = U\cap V$, $\bot=\varnothing$,
$\top=S$. (Arbitrary meets exist too, namely $\bigwedge\mathcal S = \operatorname{int}\bigcap \mathcal S$,
but we never need them.) The frame distributive law holds because it is a set-theoretic identity:
$U\cap\bigcup_{i}V_i = \bigcup_i (U\cap V_i)$.

For continuous $g : X \to Y$ let $\mathbf\Omega g : \mathbf\Omega X \to \mathbf\Omega Y$ be the
$\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism determined by
$$(\mathbf\Omega g)^{*} := g^{-1} : \mathbf\Omega Y \longrightarrow \mathbf\Omega X .$$
This is legitimate: $g^{-1}$ lands in $\mathbf\Omega X$ by continuity, and it is a frame homomorphism
because preimage commutes with arbitrary unions and with finite intersections and $g^{-1}(Y)=X$.
Functoriality follows from $(h\circ g)^{-1} = g^{-1}\circ h^{-1}$ and $\mathrm{id}^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$
together with the contravariance of $(-)^{*}$.

**The two-element frame.** $\mathbf 2 := \{\bot,\top\}$ with $\bot<\top$. It is a complete lattice, and it
is a frame: it is the topology of the one-point space (equivalently, distributivity is checked directly on
the four pairs). In $\mathbf 2$ we shall use repeatedly:
$$\bigvee T = \top \iff \top \in T \quad (T\subseteq\mathbf 2), \qquad\qquad x\wedge y = \top \iff x=y=\top. \tag{2}$$
(The first, for $T=\varnothing$, gives $\bigvee\varnothing=\bot$.)

**Points and the spectrum.** A *point* of a frame $L$ is a frame homomorphism $p : L\to\mathbf 2$;
equivalently (Remark 5) a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $\mathbf 1 \to L$ from the terminal locale
$\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 2$, equivalently a completely prime filter of $L$. Write
$$\operatorname{pt}(L) := \mathbf{Frm}(L,\mathbf 2), \qquad
\Sigma^L_a := \{\,p\in\operatorname{pt}(L) : p(a)=\top\,\}\quad (a\in L).$$
By Lemma 1, $\tau_L := \{\Sigma^L_a : a\in L\}$ is a topology on $\operatorname{pt}(L)$; the *spectrum* is
$$\operatorname{Sp}L := \bigl(\operatorname{pt}(L),\ \tau_L\bigr),$$
and for a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f : L\to M$ the map $\operatorname{Sp}f:\operatorname{Sp}L\to\operatorname{Sp}M$
is $(\operatorname{Sp}f)(p) := p\circ f^{*}$ (Lemma 3).

**The counit.** For a frame $L$, $\Sigma^L : L \to \mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$, $a\mapsto\Sigma^L_a$,
is a frame homomorphism (Lemma 2), and the component of the counit at $L$ is the $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism
$$\sigma_L : \mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\longrightarrow L, \qquad \sigma_L^{*}:=\Sigma^L .$$

**What is to be proved.** That $\sigma$ is a natural transformation
$\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}\to\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$ means exactly:

1. for each object $L$ of $\mathbf{Loc}$, $\sigma_L$ is a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism from
   $(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp})(L)$ to $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(L)=L$; and
2. for each $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f:L\to M$,
   $\ \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(f)\circ\sigma_L = \sigma_M\circ(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp})(f)$,
   i.e. $f\circ\sigma_L=\sigma_M\circ\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f$.

Item 1 is Lemma 2, item 2 is the Theorem in §4.

## 1. Lemma (the spectral topology)

**Lemma 1.** *Let $L$ be a frame. Then $\tau_L=\{\Sigma^L_a : a\in L\}$ is a topology on $\operatorname{pt}(L)$.*

*Proof.* Fix $p\in\operatorname{pt}(L)$, $a,b\in L$, $S\subseteq L$.

(a) **Joins go to unions:** $\Sigma^L_{\bigvee S}=\bigcup_{s\in S}\Sigma^L_s$.
Since $p$ is a frame homomorphism it preserves arbitrary joins, so
$p\bigl(\bigvee S\bigr)=\bigvee_{s\in S}p(s)$ — a *join* on the right, computed in $\mathbf 2$. By the
first part of $(2)$, $\bigvee_{s\in S}p(s)=\top$ iff $p(s)=\top$ for some $s\in S$. Hence
$p\in\Sigma^L_{\bigvee S}\iff \exists s\in S:\ p\in\Sigma^L_s$.

(b) **Binary meets go to intersections:** $\Sigma^L_{a\wedge b}=\Sigma^L_a\cap\Sigma^L_b$, because
$p(a\wedge b)=p(a)\wedge p(b)$ and, by the second part of $(2)$, this equals $\top$ iff
$p(a)=\top$ and $p(b)=\top$.

(c) **Units:** $\Sigma^L_{\bot_L}=\varnothing$ and $\Sigma^L_{\top_L}=\operatorname{pt}(L)$. Indeed every
point satisfies $p(\bot_L)=\bot$ and $p(\top_L)=\top$; these are precisely the empty instances of the two
preservation clauses ($S=\varnothing$ in the join clause, the empty meet in the meet clause), which is why
they were required explicitly in the definition. Note that (c) is *not* the case $S=\varnothing$ of (a)
being read off from nonempty joins: it is an independent instance, and (a) with $S=\varnothing$ reads
$\Sigma^L_{\bot_L}=\bigcup\varnothing=\varnothing$, consistently.

Now: $\varnothing,\operatorname{pt}(L)\in\tau_L$ by (c). Any subfamily of $\tau_L$ can be written as
$\{\Sigma^L_s : s\in S\}$ for some $S\subseteq L$ (choose for each member one index realising it), and its
union is $\Sigma^L_{\bigvee S}\in\tau_L$ by (a); so $\tau_L$ is closed under arbitrary unions. It is closed
under binary — hence, with (c), finite — intersections by (b). Therefore $\tau_L$ is a topology. $\blacksquare$

In particular $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L=\tau_L=\{\Sigma^L_a:a\in L\}$, a frame by the verification
given in §0 for topologies.

## 2. Lemma (each component is a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism)

**Lemma 2.** *$\Sigma^L : L\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$ is a frame homomorphism. Consequently
$\sigma_L$, defined by $\sigma_L^{*}=\Sigma^L$, is a morphism $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to L$ of
$\mathbf{Loc}$.*

*Proof.* In the frame $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$, arbitrary joins are unions, binary meets are
intersections, $\bot=\varnothing$ and $\top=\operatorname{pt}(L)$. So Lemma 1(a) says $\Sigma^L$ preserves
arbitrary joins (join to join), Lemma 1(b) says it preserves binary meets, and Lemma 1(c) says it preserves
$\bot$ and $\top$. Preservation of all finite meets follows from the binary case together with the empty
case $\Sigma^L_{\top_L}=\top$. Hence $\Sigma^L\in\mathbf{Frm}(L,\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L)$.

Because $\mathbf{Loc}=\mathbf{Frm}^{\mathrm{op}}$, an element of
$\mathbf{Frm}(L,\ \mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L)$ is precisely an element of
$\mathbf{Loc}(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L,\ L)$. So $\sigma_L$ is a well-defined $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism
with the required domain $(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp})(L)$ and codomain $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(L)=L$.
$\blacksquare$

## 3. Lemma (the spectrum of a morphism, and the key identity)

**Lemma 3.** *Let $f:L\to M$ be a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism, with underlying frame homomorphism
$f^{*}:M\to L$. Then:*

1. *$(\operatorname{Sp}f)(p):=p\circ f^{*}$ defines a map $\operatorname{pt}(L)\to\operatorname{pt}(M)$;*
2. *for every $b\in M$,*
   $$(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^M_b\bigr)\;=\;\Sigma^L_{f^{*}(b)} ;\tag{$\ast$}$$
3. *$\operatorname{Sp}f:\operatorname{Sp}L\to\operatorname{Sp}M$ is continuous.*

*Proof.* (1) If $p\in\operatorname{pt}(L)$, then $p:L\to\mathbf 2$ and $f^{*}:M\to L$ are frame
homomorphisms, hence so is the composite $p\circ f^{*}:M\to\mathbf 2$; i.e. $p\circ f^{*}\in\operatorname{pt}(M)$.

(2) Let $b\in M$ and $p\in\operatorname{pt}(L)$. Then
$$p\in(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^M_b\bigr)
\iff (\operatorname{Sp}f)(p)\in\Sigma^M_b
\iff \bigl(p\circ f^{*}\bigr)(b)=\top
\iff p\bigl(f^{*}(b)\bigr)=\top
\iff p\in\Sigma^L_{f^{*}(b)} .$$
As $p$ was arbitrary, the two sets are equal.

(3) By Lemma 1 every open set of $\operatorname{Sp}M$ has the form $\Sigma^M_b$ for some $b\in M$, and by
$(\ast)$ its preimage is $\Sigma^L_{f^{*}(b)}$, which is open in $\operatorname{Sp}L$. $\blacksquare$

*(For completeness, though not needed below: $\operatorname{Sp}$ is a functor. Indeed
$(\operatorname{Sp}\mathrm{id}_L)(p)=p\circ(\mathrm{id}_L)^{*}=p$, and for $f:L\to M$, $g:M\to N$ in
$\mathbf{Loc}$, $(\operatorname{Sp}(g\circ f))(p)=p\circ(g\circ f)^{*}=p\circ f^{*}\circ g^{*}
=(\operatorname{Sp}g)\bigl((\operatorname{Sp}f)(p)\bigr)$.)*

## 4. Theorem (naturality)

**Theorem.** *$\sigma$ is a natural transformation $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}\to\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$:
its components $\sigma_L$ are $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphisms $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to L$, and for every
$\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $f:L\to M$ the square*
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L & \xrightarrow{\ \ \sigma_L\ \ } & L\\[2pt]
{\scriptstyle\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f}\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow{\scriptstyle f}\\[2pt]
\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}M & \xrightarrow{\ \ \sigma_M\ \ } & M
\end{array}$$
*commutes in $\mathbf{Loc}$.*

*Proof.* The statement about components is Lemma 2. Let $f:L\to M$ be a $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism.

First we record the condition to be checked, in its general form, so that the two functors involved are
kept apart. For functors $F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, a family $(\sigma_C : FC\to GC)_{C\in\mathcal C}$
is natural iff
$$G(f)\circ\sigma_L \;=\; \sigma_M\circ F(f) \qquad\text{for every } f:L\to M \text{ in }\mathcal C ;$$
the *domain* functor $F$ appears on the right-hand side and the *codomain* functor $G$ on the left-hand
side — one must not write $F$ (or $G$) on both sides. Here $\mathcal C=\mathcal D=\mathbf{Loc}$,
$F=\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}$ and $G=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$, so $G(f)=f$ while
$F(f)=\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f$, and the condition is
$$f\circ\sigma_L=\sigma_M\circ\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f,$$
which is the square displayed above.

Since $(-)^{*}$ is a bijection on hom-sets reversing composition, we have the chain of equivalences
$$f\circ\sigma_L=\sigma_M\circ\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f
\iff (f\circ\sigma_L)^{*}=(\sigma_M\circ\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f)^{*}
\iff \sigma_L^{*}\circ f^{*}=(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f)^{*}\circ\sigma_M^{*},$$
an equality of maps $M\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$. (Both sides are indeed of that type: on the left,
$f^{*}:M\to L$ followed by $\sigma_L^{*}:L\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$; on the right,
$\sigma_M^{*}:M\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}M$ followed by
$(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f)^{*}:\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}M\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$.)

Now substitute the definitions: $\sigma_L^{*}=\Sigma^L$, $\sigma_M^{*}=\Sigma^M$, and, by the definition of
$\mathbf\Omega$ on morphisms applied to the continuous map $\operatorname{Sp}f$ (continuous by Lemma 3(3)),
$$(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f)^{*}=(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}.$$
So the desired identity becomes: for all $b\in M$,
$$\Sigma^L\bigl(f^{*}(b)\bigr)\;=\;(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^M(b)\bigr),
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \Sigma^L_{f^{*}(b)}=(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^M_b\bigr),$$
which is precisely $(\ast)$ of Lemma 3(2). Hence the square commutes, and $\sigma$ is a natural
transformation. $\blacksquare$

## 5. Remark (the other standard descriptions of "point")

**(i) Points as $\mathbf{Loc}$-morphisms $\mathbf 1\to L$.** The terminal locale is $\mathbf 1=\mathbf 2$
(the frame $\mathbf 2$ is initial in $\mathbf{Frm}$: a frame homomorphism $\mathbf 2\to L$ must send
$\bot\mapsto\bot_L$, $\top\mapsto\top_L$, and this map is one). By definition of $\mathbf{Loc}$, a
$\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism $q:\mathbf 1\to L$ is the same thing as a frame homomorphism $q^{*}:L\to\mathbf 2$,
so the two notions of point literally coincide. Under this identification $\operatorname{Sp}f$ is
post-composition $q\mapsto f\circ q$, whose frame translate is $q^{*}\mapsto q^{*}\circ f^{*}$ — the formula
used above. Nothing in §§1–4 changes.

**(ii) Points as completely prime filters.** Call $F\subseteq L$ a *completely prime filter* if $F$ is
up-closed, closed under binary meets, contains $\top_L$, and satisfies: $\bigvee S\in F\implies s\in F$ for
some $s\in S$ (all $S\subseteq L$). Note that properness is automatic and need not be assumed: taking
$S=\varnothing$ gives $\bot_L=\bigvee\varnothing\in F\implies(\exists s\in\varnothing)$, which is absurd, so
$\bot_L\notin F$ and hence $F\ne L$. (Conversely a filter containing $\bot_L$ would, by up-closure, be all
of $L$; so $\bot_L$ lies in no proper filter.)

The maps
$$p\longmapsto p^{-1}[\{\top\}], \qquad F\longmapsto \chi_F \ \ \bigl(\chi_F(a)=\top \text{ if } a\in F,\ \bot \text{ otherwise}\bigr)$$
are mutually inverse bijections between $\operatorname{pt}(L)$ and the set of completely prime filters of $L$.
Indeed, for $p\in\operatorname{pt}(L)$ the set $F:=p^{-1}[\{\top\}]$ is up-closed ($p$ is monotone), closed
under binary meets and contains $\top_L$ (Lemma 1(b),(c)), and is completely prime by Lemma 1(a).
Conversely, for a completely prime filter $F$ the map $\chi_F$ preserves $\top$ and binary meets (filter
conditions, using up-closure for "$\supseteq$" in $a\wedge b\in F\iff a,b\in F$) and preserves arbitrary
joins: $\chi_F(\bigvee S)=\top$ iff $\bigvee S\in F$ iff some $s\in S$ has $s\in F$ (complete primeness one
way, up-closure the other) iff $\bigvee_{s\in S}\chi_F(s)=\top$. The two constructions are visibly inverse.

Under this bijection $\Sigma^L_a$ becomes $\{F : a\in F\}$ and $\operatorname{Sp}f$ becomes
$F\mapsto (f^{*})^{-1}[F]$, and $(\ast)$ reads: $F\in(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\{G : b\in G\}$ iff
$b\in (f^{*})^{-1}[F]$ iff $f^{*}(b)\in F$. So the Theorem is insensitive to which of the three standard
presentations of "point of a locale" is adopted.

## 6. Remark (what is *not* claimed)

Naturality is a statement about commuting squares only; it uses no invertibility. Each $\sigma_L$ is a
$\mathbf{Loc}$-morphism because $\Sigma^L$ is a frame homomorphism $L\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$,
and that is all that is needed. In general $\sigma_L$ is *not* an isomorphism: $\sigma_L$ is an isomorphism
in $\mathbf{Loc}$ exactly when $\Sigma^L$ is a bijective frame homomorphism, i.e. exactly when $L$ is
spatial. (Being a frame homomorphism — even a surjective one, which $\Sigma^L$ always is by Lemma 1 — does
not make its opposite a locale isomorphism.) The theorem above is unaffected by this: it holds for all
frames $L$, spatial or not.
